title: What is wealth management?
subtitle: Net worth, asset allocation and the portfolio you expect
openingQuestion: What does wealth management actually manage first?
explanation: Wealth management is broader than portfolio management: it starts from the personal balance sheet, from goals with specific dates attached, from cash coming in and going out, and from the capacity to bear volatility. Investing is only one part, and usually not the decisive one. The two areas most often skipped, yet far more influential, are liquidity for short-term needs and protection against large risks - because one unhedged event can wipe out years of accumulation.

realWorldExample.description: A good wealth management plan does not only maximise returns; it also makes sure the money is there for education, a home, retirement, and protection against risk.

quiz.question: Where does wealth management start?
options: The target return you want to achieve each year
The list of stocks and funds currently recommended
The minimum capital needed to start investing
Net worth, goals, cash flow and risk appetite
quiz.explanation: Investing is only one part of the picture. Picking products before you know what you have, when you will need the money and how much volatility you can bear is doing it in the wrong order - the portfolio then serves itself rather than any goal. A target return chosen first is a wish, not a plan, because nothing has yet said what risk is acceptable to reach it.

quiz.question: Why does asset allocation matter more than picking the right single name?
options: Because the weights between asset classes drive most of the volatility
Because trading fees on individual names are far higher than on funds
Because names within the same asset class always move alike
Because picking the right name is something nobody can actually do
quiz.explanation: The ratio between equities, bonds and cash determines most of how much the portfolio moves. One big winner in a small part of the portfolio struggles to make up for an allocation that is wrong for your risk appetite and time horizon. Names in one class are correlated but far from identical, and some people do pick well - the point is that it matters less than the allocation.

quiz.question: Which asset is usually in the most liquid group?
options: Unlisted growth shares
Cash and bank deposits
Long-term rental property
Collectibles and precious metals
quiz.explanation: Liquidity is the first thing to establish when building a personal balance sheet. The other three all take time to convert: unlisted shares need a buyer and often a transfer approval, property takes months, and a collectible can only be sold at a fair price to the narrow set of people who want it.

quiz.question: A family will need the house fund in 3 years. Which priority is right?
options: Prioritise equities because 3 years is long term
Prioritise the highest liquidity achievable
Prioritise capital safety over growth
Prioritise growth to reach the amount in time
quiz.explanation: The same family can have three different risk appetites for three different pots: the emergency fund needs liquidity, the 3-year house fund needs capital safety, the 25-year retirement fund can bear more risk. The time horizon decides, not the age of the owner. Maximum liquidity is not the aim either - the money is not needed tomorrow, it is needed on a known date.

quiz.question: What is the point of rebalancing a portfolio?
options: Shifting gradually into safer assets
Selling the poor assets and keeping the good ones
Raising the expected return of the whole portfolio
Keeping the risk level chosen at the outset
quiz.explanation: Without rebalancing, a portfolio drifts away from the risk appetite it started with, because whatever has risen most now occupies the largest weight. It is not a judgement about which asset is good or poor - rebalancing usually means selling some of the winner - and it is a discipline about risk rather than a way to lift returns.

quiz.question: Why does a good plan not aim only at maximising returns?
options: Because short-term liquidity and sudden risks still need covering
Because maximising returns only applies to institutional investors
Because regulators cap the return an investor is allowed to enjoy
Because a high return always brings a higher tax bill with it
quiz.explanation: A high-returning portfolio with no cash for the next six months' needs will force a sale at exactly the wrong moment. Protection against events and enough liquidity are the conditions that let the long-term investment run undisturbed. Tax is a real cost but it is a deduction from a good outcome, not a reason to avoid one.

keyTakeaways: Wealth management looks at net worth first, and only then at investing
Asset allocation matters more than picking one winning name
Rebalancing keeps the risk discipline in place

practicePrompt.question: What is the core goal of the wealth management industry for an individual client?
options: Preserving capital, sustainable growth, optimal asset allocation
Advising the client to bet their whole net worth on one momentum stock
Promising a fixed 50% annual return with no risk
Selling insurance products at any cost
practicePrompt.explanation: Wealth management focuses on managing the whole financial picture: retirement planning, diversified asset allocation (equities, bonds, property) and protecting wealth across generations.

summary.keyIdea: Wealth management looks at net worth first, and only then at investing
summary.commonMistake: Easy to miss: asset allocation matters more than picking one winning name
summary.action: Rebalancing keeps the risk discipline in place

application.title: Map out your net worth
application.message: List your assets, debts, cash, investments and upcoming goals in one simple table, so you know which part needs protecting first.
application.secondary: Usually liquidity and a safety buffer matter more than the maximum return.

sections.text: Wealth management is not something 'you only need once you have a lot of money'. It is how you organise assets, risk and goals so that money serves your life.

sections.title: The wealth management framework
sections.subtitle: Read left to right as a process

concepts.def: Total assets less total debts - the starting point of every plan.
Dividing money across cash, bonds, equities, property and so on, according to the goals.
Bringing the portfolio back to its target weights as markets move.

left.label: The common mistake
left.text: Seeing one high-returning channel and pouring money into it without considering the goal, the liquidity or the time frame.

right.label: The right approach
right.text: Dividing assets by goal: money for the near term, money for protection, money for growth, money for the long term.

sections.text: A concrete example: a family with a net worth of VND 5bn, with goals including an emergency fund (highly liquid, 6 months of spending), a house fund for the next 3 years (safety first), and a retirement fund 25 years out (able to bear more risk for growth). Wealth management properly done means allocating that VND 5bn into three different 'pots' according to the time frame and goal of each, instead of pooling it and investing all of it on a single strategy.
Splitting that VND 5bn into three pots, each with its own risk appetite

The family spends VND 30m a month, so a 6-month emergency fund is VND 180m - 3.6% of their assets. The house deposit needs VND 1.5bn in 3 years, which is 30%. The remaining VND 3.32bn, or 66.4%, is retirement money with a 20-year horizon. These three pots cannot share one equity weighting, because what decides it is not how adventurous the family is but when the money has to be there.

sections.title: One family, three different levels of risk
sections.subtitle: The time horizon decides, not the personality

concepts.vi: Emergency fund - VND 180m, needed at any moment
concepts.def: The only criterion is being able to withdraw immediately without losing value. Short-term deposits or a money market fund. Putting a single dong of equity in here means accepting you may have to sell at a loss precisely when you lose your job.

concepts.vi: House deposit - VND 1.5bn, needed in 3 years
concepts.def: Three years is too short to wait out a recovery from a fall. If the market drops 30% in the third year, the plan to buy is postponed - and that is a real failure, not a temporary fluctuation.

This is the only pot long enough for volatility risk to become something you are paid for. Keeping this pot too safe is the biggest risk of all, because 20 years of inflation erodes purchasing power more certainly than any market fall.

sections.label: Why asking what your risk appetite is out of ten is usually meaningless
sections.text: The same person, on the same day, has three different answers for the three pots above. Collapsing them into one number and applying a single allocation to the whole VND 5bn puts the emergency fund somewhere too risky and the retirement money somewhere too safe - wrong at both ends at once. That is why asset allocation starts from a list of goals with dates attached, not from a personality questionnaire.

lines: Good wealth management is there to make life hold fewer surprises.
Not to chase the prettiest return figure.
